title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-285-632-002
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-285-632-002
Issue
Whether Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence that the
right foot reconstruction surgery recommended by authorized treating physician (ATP)
Stuart Myers, MD is reasonable, necessary, and causally related to her August 25, 2024
industrial injury.
Findings of Fact
1. On August 25, 2024 Claimant was working as a respiratory therapist on the
Medical/Surgical Acute Care Unit at Employer’s hospital when the code blue alarm was
activated. While running to respond to the code as part of her job duties, Claimant
experienced a sudden pop or pull sensation in her right foot and ankle. She immediately
experienced acute pain.
2. On September 25, 2024 Claimant underwent a right foot MRI with Shayan
Vadie, MD at Spectrum Medical Imaging. The MRI revealed moderate posterior tibialis
tendinosis and tenosynovitis with low-grade partial-thickness interstitial tearing, along
with mild subcutaneous soft tissue edema along the medial ankle.
3. On October 7, 2024 Claimant underwent an initial occupational medical
evaluation with Christian Updike, MD at UCHealth Occupational Medicine. He diagnosed
a severe ankle strain with small tears and determined the mechanism of injury was
consistent with Claimant’s work activities.
4. On October 30, 2024 Claimant visited Stuart Myers, MD for an initial
orthopedic evaluation of her right ankle. Dr. Myers noted that Claimant had been wearing
a boot provided by occupational medicine. However, she continued to experience pain
after 5-6 hours of walking. Dr. Myers diagnosed Claimant with tibial tendon dysfunction.
He recommended orthotics and bracing.
5. On December 4, 2024 Claimant began undergoing physical therapy at
CACC Physical Therapy.

6. Claimant returned to Dr. Myers on December 11, 2024. She reported
continuing pain in her right ankle after 3-4 hours of walking with a lace up brace. Dr. Myers
recommended PRP injections to the right ankle.
7. On January 27, 2025 Dr. Myers administered Claimant’s first PRP injection
under ultrasound guidance into the posterior tibial tendon sheath. On May 5, 2025
Claimant underwent a second PRP injection because of partial but incomplete relief from
the first injection. Later in May 2025 Claimant received a third PRP injection. However, it
also did not provide significant relief.
8. Despite the preceding extensive conservative treatment spanning more
than one year, Claimant continued to experience persistent pain, swelling, the inability to
perform a single-leg heel rise, and an antalgic gait. As of her follow-up appointment with
Dr. Myers on January 6, 2026, she continued to have ankle pain and swelling, was unable
to perform a single-leg heel rise and remained unable to return to work.
9. On October 13, 2025 Respondents retained Nathan C. Hammel, MD to
conduct a records review of Claimant’s claim. Dr. Hammel agreed that the partial
thickness tear from Claimant’s September MRI and her more recent medical records
revealed consistency between the mechanism of injury and her symptoms. He was not
certain if Claimant had reached maximum medical improvement (MMI), although he
thought she had been improving and could be eased back into her regular job duties. Dr.
Hammel recommended additional PRP injections because they provided objective benefit
as measured by reduction in immobilization and decreasing pain scores.
10. In response to Dr. Hammel’s records review report, Respondents filed a
general admission of liability (GAL) on November 7, 2025 recognizing that she was
injured on August 25, 2024.
11. On December 29, 2025 Claimant underwent a repeat MRI of the right ankle.
Douglas Watt, MD remarked that the imaging revealed a full-thickness tear of the
posterior tibial tendon. The imaging reflects progression from the partial-thickness
interstitial tear identified in September 2024.
12. On January 6, 2026 Dr. Myers reviewed the December 29, 2025 MRI and
recommended surgical reconstruction of the right foot. The complete tear of the posterior
tibial tendon could not be repaired by simple suturing. Expected recovery included six
2

weeks of non-weight bearing, followed by one month in a walking boot and transitioning
to a lace-up brace.
13. On January 10, 2026 Respondents obtained a second records review from
Dr. Hammel. He determined that, while the right foot reconstruction surgery is reasonable
and necessary, it is not causally related to Claimant’s work injury. Dr. Hammel reasoned
that, because Claimant has remained off work since the date of injury and the tendon
progressed to a full-thickness tear, the change was attributable to a pre-existing
degenerative condition. He further remarked that the initial MRI showing tendinosis
reflected a "chronic pre-existing degenerative condition," and the work injury only caused
the acute tenosynovitis component.
14. On April 6, 2026 Respondents conducted the post-hearing evidentiary
deposition of Dr. Hammel. Dr. Hammel explained that Claimant initially suffered from
posterior tibial tendonitis. This was based on his review of Claimant’s MRI that showed
fluid around the posterior tibial tendon and its tendon sheath. Claimant’s flat-footedness
was a pre-existing, degenerative, condition that would lead to an eventual full-thickness,
acute-type injury. PRP injections benefited Claimant because they appeared to have the
effect of muting an acute inflammatory response.
15. Dr. Hammel testified that Claimant’s December 29, 2025 MRI showed a full-
thickness tear across the posterior tibial tendon with retraction. He explained that the
initial September 25, 2024 MRI had revealed interstitial partial tearing of the same tendon,
similar to a rope bundle that is beginning to fray. On the original MRI, the rope bundle
was still intact, though there were parts of the outside of the rope that were beginning to
fray. However, by the time of the second MRI in December 2025, the rope had entirely
snapped and was thus no longer functioning.
16. Based on Claimant’s December 2025 MRI findings, Dr. Hammel determined
her condition was not causally related to the work injury. The interstitial partial thickness
tearing was a pre-existing, degenerative condition that progressed to a full-thickness
rupture.
17. Dr. Hammel further explained that the progression of an underlying pre-
existing condition, in the absence of continued trauma or a second injury, reflects that
Claimant’s rupture was from the progression of the underlying condition. The type of
3

progression could be caused by simply walking or stair climbing. Dr. Hammel concluded
that Claimant’s original work injury did not worsen or accelerate Claimant’s degenerative
process.
18. On March 16, 2026 Claimant underwent an independent medical
examination (IME) with Mark Winslow, DO. He concluded that Claimant’s progression
from a partial-thickness tear to a full-thickness tear was the direct result of her August 25,
2024 work-related injury. Dr. Winslow detailed the following:
• Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction is a progressive condition, involving
degenerative tendinosis with disruption in collagen bundle structure and
orientation. It compromises the tendon and predisposes it to rupture under
physiologic loads.
• The hypovascularity of the posterior tibial tendon in the region behind the medial
malleolus predisposes this region specifically to degenerative disorders and
rupture.
• The progression of a partial tear to a complete tear does not require additional
trauma. The pathologic changes in posterior tibial tendon dysfunction can lead to
tendon degeneration with an insufficient repair response, culminating in rupture
under normal activities of daily living and not just occupational activities.
Claimant’s physical examination findings including significant acquired pronation
of the right foot since the date of injury, antalgic gait, medial arch tenderness, pain
with resisted dorsiflexion, and asymmetric shoe wear on the right are consistent
with progressive posterior tibial tendon dysfunction.
19. Dr. Winslow explained that the present matter “presents a clinically
straightforward progression of a work-related posterior tibial tendon injury.” He recounted
that Claimant sustained an acute injury at work on August 25, 2024 to a previously
asymptomatic foot. An MRI revealed a partial-thickness tear of the posterior tibial tendon.
Despite conservative treatment, including rest, immobilization, physical therapy, and
three PRP injections, her symptoms persisted and the tear progressed to a complete, full
thickness rupture as documented on the December 2025 MRI.
20. Dr. Winslow noted that the denial of surgery is based on the opinion that the
progression of the tear was unrelated to the original injury because Claimant was not
4

working during the time when the tear progressed. However, Dr. Winslow commented
that the reasoning is not supported by the medical literature regarding the natural history
of posterior tibial tendon dysfunction.
21. Dr. Winslow maintained that Claimant’s absence from work was irrelevant
to a causation analysis. Notably, the posterior tibial tendon functions as the main dynamic
stabilizing tendon of the medial longitudinal arch. It absorbs shock during heel strike,
stabilizes the foot during midstance, and generates force during heel and toe lift. The
preceding functions are required for basic ambulation, not just occupational activities. The
tendon was thus under a physiologic load throughout Claimant’s activities of daily living
regardless of her work status.
22. Dr. Winslow also noted that Claimant’s treating physicians, Dr. Updike and
Dr. Myers, have consistently maintained that Claimant’s condition constitutes a
progression of the initial work injury and have recommended surgery. Their opinions are
consistent with the established medical literature on the natural history of posterior tibial
tendon dysfunction. Notably, Dr. Winslow remarked that the medical literature supports
surgical intervention for complete posterior tibial tendon tears when conservative
treatment has failed after three to six months. Notably, Claimant underwent more than a
year of conservative treatment including immobilization, physical therapy, and three PRP
injections without achieving adequate relief or functional improvement.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
1. The purpose of the “Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado” (Act) is to
assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical benefits to injured workers
at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of any litigation. §8-40-102(1),
C.R.S. A claimant in a Workers' Compensation claim has the burden of proving
entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. §8-42-101, C.R.S. A
preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering all of
the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 197 Colo.
306, 592 P.2d 792 (1979); People v. M.A., 104 P.3d 273, 275 (Colo. App. 2004). The
5

facts in a Workers' Compensation case are not interpreted liberally in favor of either the
rights of the injured worker or the rights of the employer. §8-43-201, C.R.S. A Workers'
Compensation case is decided on its merits. §8-43-201, C.R.S.
2. The Judge’s factual findings concern only evidence that is dispositive of the
issues involved; the Judge has not addressed every piece of evidence that might lead to
a conflicting conclusion and has rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as
unpersuasive. See Magnetic Engineering, Inc. v. ICAO, 5 P.3d 385, 389 (Colo. App.
2000).
3. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions; the
reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the testimony and
actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has been contradicted; and
bias, prejudice, or interest. See Prudential Insurance Co. v. Cline, 98 Colo. 275, 57 P.2d
1205 (1936); CJI, Civil 3:16 (2007).
4. Respondents are liable for authorized medical treatment that is reasonable
and necessary to cure or relieve the effects of an industrial injury. §8-42101(1)(a), C.R.S.;
Colorado Comp. Ins. Auth. v. Nofio, 886 P.2d 714, 716 (Colo. 1994). A pre-existing
condition or susceptibility to injury does not disqualify a claim if the employment
aggravates, accelerates, or combines with the pre-existing condition to produce a need
for medical treatment. Duncan v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 107 P.3d 999, 1001 (Colo.
App. 2004). The question of whether a particular disability is the result of the natural
progression of a pre-existing condition, or the subsequent aggravation or acceleration of
that condition, is itself a question of fact. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Off., 43 P.3d 637 (Colo. App. 2001). Finally, the determination of whether a
particular treatment modality is reasonable and necessary to treat an industrial injury is a
factual determination for the ALJ. In re Parker, W.C. No. 4-517-537 (ICAO, May 31, 2006);
In re Frazier, W.C. No. 3-920-202 (ICAO, Nov. 13, 2000).
5. Section 8-41-301(1)(c), C.R.S. requires that an injury be “proximately
caused by an injury or occupational disease arising out of and in the course of the
employee’s employment.” Thus, the claimant is required to prove a direct causal
6

relationship between the injury and the disability and need for treatment. However, the
industrial injury need not be the sole cause of the disability if the injury is a significant,
direct, and consequential factor in the disability. See Subsequent Injury Fund v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 131 P.3d 1224 (Colo. App. 2006); Joslins Dry Goods Co. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 21 P.3d 866 (Colo. App. 2001).
6. Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence that the right
foot reconstruction surgery recommended by ATP Dr. Myers is reasonable, necessary,
and causally related to her August 25, 2024 industrial injury. Initially, on August 25, 2024,
while running to respond to an emergency at work, Claimant experienced a sudden pop
or pull sensation in her right foot and ankle. A September 25, 2024 MRI of Claimant’s
right foot revealed moderate posterior tibialis tendinosis and tenosynovitis with low-grade
partial-thickness interstitial tearing. Claimant subsequently underwent extensive
conservative treatment including physical therapy and three PRP injections.
Nevertheless, Claimant continued to experience persistent pain and swelling. On
December 29, 2025 Claimant underwent a repeat MRI of the right ankle that revealed a
full-thickness tear of the posterior tibial tendon. The imaging documented progression
from the partial-thickness interstitial tear identified in September 2024. The resolution of
the present matter is contingent on whether the progression from a partial to a full-
thickness tear is causally connected to Claimant’s initial work injury on August 25, 2024
or constituted the natural progression of a pre-existing condition. Based on the
determinations of Claimant’s treating physicians and the persuasive opinion of Dr.
Winslow, Claimant’s full-thickness tear and need for surgery are causally related to her
August 25, 2024 industrial injury.
7. Both of Claimant’s treating physicians have repeatedly attributed her
condition to the August 25, 2024 work injury. They have examined Claimant and reviewed
her diagnostic imaging. Dr. Updike documented at each visit from October 2024 through
December 2025 that the mechanism of injury was consistent with a work-related incident.
Dr. Myers diagnosed a right ankle work injury at every encounter from October 2024
through January 2026 and has recognized the relationship between the injury and
Claimant’s continuing condition. He recommended surgical reconstruction of the right
7

foot. The complete tear of the posterior tibial tendon could not be repaired by simple
suturing.
8. In contrast, Dr. Hammel determined that, while the recommended right foot
reconstruction surgery is reasonable and necessary, it is not causally related to
Claimant’s work injury. He reasoned that, because Claimant has remained off work since
the date of injury and the tendon progressed to a full-thickness tear, the progression was
attributable to a pre-existing degenerative condition. Dr. Hammel remarked that the
progression of an underlying, pre-existing condition, in the absence of continued trauma
or a second injury, reflects that Claimant’s rupture was from the advancement of the
underlying condition. The type of worsening could be caused by simply walking or stair
climbing. Dr. Hammel concluded that Claimant’s original work injury did not worsen or
accelerate the degenerative process.
9. Despite Dr. Hammel’s conclusion, Dr. Winslow agreed with Claimant’s
treating physicians and determined that the progression from a partial-thickness tear to a
full-thickness tear was the direct result of Claimant’s August 25, 2024 work-related injury.
Dr. Winslow noted that the denial of surgery was based on the view that the progression
of the tear was unrelated to the original injury because Claimant was not working during
the time when the tear worsened. However, the preceding reasoning is not supported by
the medical literature regarding the natural history of posterior tibial tendon dysfunction.
10. Dr. Winslow remarked that posterior tibial tendon dysfunction is a
progressive condition, involving degenerative tendinosis with disruption in collagen
bundle structure and orientation. Despite conservative treatment, including rest,
immobilization, physical therapy, and three PRP injections, Claimant’s symptoms
persisted and the tear progressed to a complete, full thickness rupture as documented on
the December 2025 MRI. Dr. Winslow noted that Claimant’s treating physicians, Dr.
Updike and Dr. Myers, have consistently maintained that Claimant’s condition constitutes
a progression of the initial work injury and recommended surgery. Their opinions follow
the established medical literature on the natural history of posterior tibial tendon
dysfunction. Notably, Dr. Winslow remarked that the medical literature supports surgical
intervention for complete posterior tibial tendon tears when conservative treatment has
failed after three to six months.
8

11. The progression of Claimant’s posterior tibial tendon injury from a partial to
a complete tear is the natural and expected consequence of her August 25, 2024 work
injury. Claimant’s treating physicians and Dr. Winslow support the preceding conclusion.
Respondent’s denial of Claimant’s surgical request is based on a paper review by a
physician who has never examined her and whose causation reasoning is contrary to
established medical literature. Accordingly, Claimant’s full-thickness tear and need for
surgery is reasonable, necessary and causally related to her August 25, 2024 industrial
injury. Claimant’s request for the right foot reconstruction surgery recommended by Dr.
Myers is thus authorized.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant has demonstrated that the right foot reconstruction surgery
recommended by Dr. Myers is authorized, reasonable, necessary, and causally related
to her August 25, 2024 industrial injury.
2. All matters not resolved in this Order are resolved for future determination.
9

If you are dissatisfied with the Judge's order, you may file a Petition to Review the
order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on certificate of mailing or service; otherwise,
the Judge's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as long as the
certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it within twenty
(20) days after mailing or service of the order of the Judge; and (2) That you mailed it to
the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. For statutory reference,
see section 8-43-301(2), C.R.S. For further information regarding procedures to follow
when filing a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may access a petition to
review form at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.
Dated: May 14, 2026 _

Peter J. Cannici
Administrative Law Judge

Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. 5-272-096-002
Based on the evidence presented at hearing, it is hereby ordered:
1. The respondents are liable for medical treatment reasonably needed to
cure and relieve the effects of an industrial injury. Section 8-42-101, C.R.S. The mere
occurrence of a compensable injury does not compel the ALJ to approve all requested
treatment. Where the claimant’s entitlement to medical benefits is disputed, the claimant
must prove the treatment is reasonably needed and causally related to the industrial
accident. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 989 P.2d 251 (Colo.
App. 1999). The claimant must prove entitlement to disputed medical benefits by a
preponderance of the evidence. Snyder v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 942 P.2d
1337 (Colo. App. 1997).
2. Claimant proved the TFCC surgery recommended by Dr. Larsen is
reasonably needed and causally related to the work accident. Claimant suffered an
admitted injury on March 31, 2024, when she struck her right arm on a dumpster while
throwing trash. The impact was corroborated by a cut on her right forearm. An MRI
within a month of the accident showed a TFCC tear and an effusion consistent with a
relatively recent, traumatic injury. Dr. Larsen’s opinions are credible and more
persuasive than the contrary opinions of Dr. Worrell. Dr. Larsen credibly opined that the
precise motion of Claimant’s arm when it impacted the dumpster is not critical to a
determination of causation. There is no persuasive evidence of any pre-existing right
wrist or forearm problems, nor of any alternate causal factor besides the work accident.
Dr. Larsen credibly opined that Claimant has exhausted conservative treatment and
surgery is the reasonable next step.
3. Insurer shall cover the TFCC surgery recommended by Dr. Larsen.
1

4. As stipulated, Insurer shall pay Claimant temporary partial disability (TPD)
benefits in the amount of $1,771.71, based on an average weekly wage of $857.19.
5. All matters not decided herein are reserved for future determination.
Dated: May 22, 2026 /s/ Patrick C.H. Spencer II
Administrative Law Judge
This decision is final and not subject to appeal unless a full order is requested. The
request shall be made at the Office of Administrative Courts, 1330 Inverness Drive, Suite
330, Colorado Springs, CO 80910 within ten working days of the date of service of this
Summary Order. Section 8-43-215(1), C.R.S. Such a request is a prerequisite to review
under § 8-43-301, C.R.S.
Pursuant to OACRP 26(B), if either party requests a full order, both parties shall
submit a proposed order containing specific findings of fact and conclusions of law within
seven days from the date of the request. The proposed full order must be submitted by
e-mail in Word format to oac-csp@state.co.us The proposed order shall also be submitted
to opposing counsel and unrepresented parties by e-mail, or same day or next day
delivery.
